content_html:
About

A Rust SDK for writing custom backends for NVIDIA Triton Inference Server. Backends run as shared libraries inside Triton. The project also includes an async gRPC client for calling a running Triton server.

Targets Triton 25.09 / backend API 1.19 and Rust 1.99. The API checks compatibility at backend startup. The examples below describe the 0.4.0 API. See CHANGELOG for release boundaries.

Crate Description
triton-ng Safe backend API
triton-ng-client Async gRPC client
triton-ng-sys Raw FFI bindings
triton-ng-macros Backend and batching entry points

Getting started

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
triton-ng = "0.4.0"

Implement one hook to call another model and return its output. This complete backend is also examples/minimal-backend, the minimal backend example (the separate batching-strategy example is introduced below):

use triton_ng::{Context, CustomBackend, DataType, Error, InferenceRequest, Request, Response};

struct MyBackend;

#[triton_ng::backend]
impl CustomBackend for MyBackend {
    async fn model_instance_execute(ctx: Context, requests: Vec<Request>) -> Result<(), Error> {
        for request in requests {
            let data = request.get_input("INPUT")?.as_bytes()?;

            let mut inference = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
            inference.add_input_with_data("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], data)?;
            inference.add_requested_output("OUTPUT0")?;
            let result = match ctx.server().infer_async(inference).await {
                Ok(result) => result,
                Err(e) => {
                    request.respond_error_with_code(e.code(), &e.to_string())?;
                    continue;
                }
            };

            let mut response = Response::new(request)?;
            response
                .create_output("OUTPUT", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10])?
                .write_fp32_vec(&result.output("OUTPUT0")?.as_fp32_vec()?)?;
            response.send()?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

gRPC client

Call the custom backend from your application using the gRPC client:

use triton_ng_client::{InferInput, InferOptions, TritonClient, TritonClientConfig};

type ClientError = Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>;

async fn call_example() -> Result<(), ClientError> {
    let client = TritonClient::new(TritonClientConfig::new("http://localhost:8001")).await?;
    let result = client.infer(
        "minimal_backend", None,
        [InferInput::fp32("INPUT", vec![1, 10], vec![1.0; 10])],
        ["OUTPUT"], InferOptions::default(),
    ).await?;
    for output in result.outputs {
        println!("{}: {:?}", output.name, output.data);
    }
    Ok(())
}

The examples below are independent functions or hooks; import their SDK types from triton_ng. Combine state fields when using several examples in one backend. make build compile-checks the Rust snippets in this README and every guide.

Compose models with BLS

Forward an input to another model without copying it:

async fn forward_input(ctx: &Context, request: &Request) -> Result<InferenceResult, Error> {
    let shared = request.get_input("INPUT")?.share()?;
    let mut call = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
    call.add_input_with_buffer("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], shared)?;
    call.add_requested_output("OUTPUT0")?;
    Ok(ctx.server().infer_async(call).await?)
}

To replace an input prepared by another helper and request only the embedding:

fn replace_audio(call: &mut InferenceRequest, samples: i64, audio: Vec<u8>) -> Result<(), Error> {
    call.remove_input("AUDIO")?;
    call.add_input_with_data("AUDIO", DataType::Fp32, &[1, samples], audio)?;
    call.remove_all_requested_outputs()?;
    call.add_requested_output("EMBEDDING")?;
    Ok(())
}

Request editing and buffer lifetimes.

Streaming

Return tokens as they become available. Configure the model with model_transaction_policy { decoupled: true }:

fn send_tokens(request: Request) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut sender = request.into_sender()?;
    for token in [10, 20, 30] {
        let mut response = sender.response()?;
        response.create_output("TOKEN", DataType::Int32, &[1])?.write_i32_vec(&[token])?;
        response.send()?;
    }
    sender.finish()?;
    Ok(())
}

Call a streaming model from another backend with Server::infer_stream, or from an application with TritonClient::infer_stream. See streaming and cancellation for complete examples.

Metrics and response statistics

Count completed requests on Triton's Prometheus endpoint. Create the counter once in model initialization and call count_request from execute:

fn model_initialize(model: &Model) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let name = model.name()?;
    let counter = CounterFamily::new("minimal_requests_total", "Requests handled")?
        .counter(&[("model", name.as_str())])?;
    model.set_state(counter)?;
    Ok(())
}

fn count_request(ctx: &Context) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ctx.state::<Counter>()?.increment(1.0)?;
    Ok(())
}

Request and batch statistics are automatic. Enable per-response statistics when needed:

fn answer_with_statistics(request: Request) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut response = Response::new(request)?;
    response.create_output("OUTPUT", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10])?.write_fp32_vec(&[0.0; 10])?;
    response.enable_statistics();
    response.send()?;
    Ok(())
}

Metric types, error responses, and statistics.

Tracing and metadata

Add a trace activity and connect a BLS call to its client request:

async fn traced_call(ctx: &Context, request: &Request) -> Result<InferenceResult, Error> {
    request.trace()?.report_activity("decode")?;
    let mut call = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
    call.set_parent_trace(request)?;
    if let Some(id) = request.id()? { call.set_id(&id)?; }
    call.set_parameter("language", "en")?;
    call.add_input_with_data("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], request.get_input("INPUT")?.as_bytes()?)?;
    Ok(ctx.server().infer_async(call).await?)
}

Request IDs, sequence flags, priority, timeouts, and tracing.

Memory buffers

Choose memory for each output, then take the buffers back for reuse. This example takes a prepared request for a model with three FP32 outputs of shape [1, 10]:

async fn reuse_outputs(
    ctx: &Context,
    mut call: InferenceRequest,
    device_id: i32,
) -> Result<(RamBuffer, PinnedRamBuffer, GpuBuffer), Error> {
    call.add_requested_output_into("CPU_OUTPUT", ctx.memory().ram(40)?)?;
    call.add_requested_output_into("PINNED_OUTPUT", ctx.memory().pinned(40)?)?;
    call.add_requested_output_into("GPU_OUTPUT", ctx.memory().gpu(device_id, 40)?)?;
    let mut result = ctx.server().infer_async(call).await?;
    Ok((
        result.take_ram("CPU_OUTPUT")?,
        result.take_pinned("PINNED_OUTPUT")?,
        result.take_gpu("GPU_OUTPUT")?,
    ))
}

Use any one of these buffer types, or combine them as above. Pinned and GPU allocations require Triton's corresponding memory pools. A GpuBuffer can become the next BLS call's input without a host copy; CPU access to its data requires your own CUDA code.

Report memory held by your model so clients can inspect it in model statistics:

fn model_initialize(model: &Model) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let allocation = model.memory_manager()?.pinned(4096)?;
    model.set_state(allocation)?;
    model.report_memory_usage(&[BufferAttributes::new(MemoryType::CpuPinned, 4096)?])?;
    Ok(())
}

For per-instance allocations use ModelInstance::report_memory_usage. Memory ownership, GPU chaining, and caching.

Configure backend and instances

Keep a setting shared by every model of your backend:

fn initialize(backend: &Backend) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let language = backend.config()?.parameter_or("language", String::from("en"))?;
    backend.set_state(language)?;
    backend.set_execution_policy(ExecutionPolicy::Blocking)?;
    let (_, directory) = backend.artifacts()?;
    println!("Backend files: {}", directory.display());
    Ok(())
}

fn language(ctx: &Context) -> Result<&str, Error> {
    Ok(ctx.backend_state::<String>()?.as_str())
}

Inspect an instance and save its host policy for later input reads:

fn model_instance_initialize(instance: &ModelInstance) -> Result<(), Error> {
    println!("{} passive={} profiles={:?} secondary={:?}",
        instance.name()?, instance.is_passive()?, instance.profile_names()?, instance.secondary_devices()?);
    instance.set_state(instance.host_policy()?)?;
    Ok(())
}

Backend configuration, execution policies, and instance settings.

Host-policy input data

Read the input storage selected for this instance:

fn read_policy(ctx: &Context, request: &Request) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Error> {
    let policy = ctx.instance_state::<HostPolicy>()?;
    request.get_input("INPUT")?.as_bytes_for_host_policy(policy.name())
}

Supply different input bytes for a BLS target's host policy:

fn policy_call(ctx: &Context, default: Vec<u8>, local: &[u8]) -> Result<InferenceRequest, Error> {
    let mut call = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
    call.add_input_with_data("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], default)?;
    call.append_input_data_with_host_policy("INPUT0", local, "cpu")?;
    Ok(call)
}

Each input above contains ten FP32 values (40 bytes). A policy without supplied data uses the ordinary input. Policy selection and zero-copy appends.

Sequence state and iterative requests

Count requests in a sequence. Declare a state tensor with an initial value of zero, read its StateConfig with Model::sequence_states, then update it on each request:

fn increment(mut request: Request, config: &StateConfig) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let previous = request.get_input(config.input_name())?.as_fp32_vec()?;
    let previous = previous.first().copied().ok_or("state has no counter")?;
    let mut state = State::new(&mut request, config, &[1])?;
    state.write_bytes(&(previous + 1.0).to_ne_bytes())?;
    state.update()?;
    let mut response = Response::new(request)?;
    response.create_output("OUTPUT", DataType::Fp32, &[1])?.write_fp32_vec(&[previous + 1.0])?;
    response.send()?;
    Ok(())
}

This example uses max_batch_size: 0 and state dimensions [1]. Complete sequence-state configuration.

Return a partial result and schedule another step of a decoupled iterative sequence:

fn next_step(request: Request) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut sender = request.into_sender()?;
    let mut response = sender.response()?;
    response.create_output("STEP", DataType::Int32, &[1])?.write_i32_vec(&[1])?;
    response.send()?;
    sender.reschedule()?;
    Ok(())
}

Triton r25.09 allows only one reschedule per request; finish the response on the second step. Two-step execution and model configuration.

Custom batching

Group adjacent requests with the same batch_key parameter:

struct ByKey;
struct Batch { started: bool, key: Option<String> }

#[triton_ng::batch_strategy]
impl BatchStrategy for ByKey {
    type Batch = Batch;
    fn initialize(_model: &Model) -> Result<Self, Error> { Ok(Self) }
    fn batch(&self) -> Batch { Batch { started: false, key: None } }
    fn include(&self, batch: &mut Batch, request: &RequestView<'_>) -> Result<bool, Error> {
        let key = match request.parameter("batch_key")? {
            Some(Parameter::String(value)) => Some(value),
            _ => None,
        };
        if !batch.started {
            batch.started = true;
            batch.key = key;
            return Ok(true);
        }
        Ok(batch.key == key)
    }
}

Build this as a separate library and set TRITON_BATCH_STRATEGY_PATH in the model config. Runnable example · Queue behavior and safe model unload.

Comparison with python_backend

Against python_backend r25.09:

Area python_backend triton-ng
Runtime Python stub process per instance; shared-memory communication Rust shared library in the Triton process
BLS exec / async_exec, decoupled iterator infer_async futures and infer_stream
Streaming Response sender and final flags Consuming ResponseSender and typed response ownership
Memory NumPy, DLPack and CUDA IPC Owned RAM/pinned/GPU buffers; shared request inputs
Isolation A model crash generally affects its stub Panics are contained; a native crash affects Triton
Best fit Python/framework code inside the backend Typed orchestration around Triton framework models

Full comparison, including feature gaps and cases where Python is the better choice.

Benchmarks

The recorded benchmark compares five small BLS workloads on the same Triton 25.09 server, two CPU instances per backend, with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D. At concurrency 64:

Workload triton-ng requests/s python_backend requests/s Ratio
Argmax, no BLS 119,907 52,716 2.27×
One BLS call 43,422 17,819 2.44×
Concurrent BLS calls 74,316 13,317 5.58×
Decoupled responses 12,802 3,670 3.49×
Consuming a BLS stream 15,056 3,253 4.63×

These are the recorded measurements, not a promise for large GPU models; heavy inference reduces the backend's share of total time. Streaming latency in these results is time to first response. Method, environment, all concurrency levels, and latency tables are in the benchmark guide.

Documentation

Start with the topics you need; the guides and this README are also included in the Rust API documentation.

Guide What you will learn
Execution model and thread safety Instances and their threads, state of models and instances, request ownership, error codes, BLS futures, threads, cancellation, shutdown, batching
Batching and concurrency How Triton forms batches and why a batch runs on the Triton thread of its instance, BLS calls joined inside a batch, tuning with instance_group, measurements
Streaming Decoupled models: streams of responses from a backend, BLS streams, cancellation of BLS calls, the client side, how it is implemented and its limitations
Model parameters The parameters map of a model config and how a backend reads it
Request metadata and tracing ID, correlation ID, sequence flags and timeout of a request; setting them, the priority and parameters on BLS calls; BLS calls as children of the trace of a request
Metrics Counters, gauges and histograms of the backend on Triton's Prometheus endpoint; the inference statistics triton-ng reports for every model
Model management and configuration The backend config from --backend-config, backend attributes (preferred instance groups, parallel instance loading), completing model configs, loading and unloading models from a backend, rescheduling requests of iterative sequences, the state a sequence keeps between its requests
Memory buffers RAM, pinned and GPU buffers from Triton's memory manager for BLS inputs and outputs, caching them in a backend, passing inputs of a request on without a copy, reporting the memory a model and its instances hold
C API coverage All 276 C functions: Rust and Python coverage, public APIs, internal support, and missing wrappers
Benchmarks python_backend and triton-ng on the same BLS workloads with perf_analyzer: method, models, environment, results
python_backend comparison Runtime differences, feature coverage, isolation, and when to use Python

Development

Install Rust, Docker, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and a compatible NVIDIA driver. The test suite also requires cargo-nextest. From the repository root:

make build
make download-model
make docker-env-up
make tests
make docker-env-down

Wait until Triton reports the models ready before running the tests. After changing a backend, rebuild and restart the service. See the Makefile for all development commands.

License

MIT

content_html_zh:
About

A Rust SDK for writing custom backends for NVIDIA Triton Inference Server. Backends run as shared libraries inside Triton. The project also includes an async gRPC client for calling a running Triton server.

Targets Triton 25.09 / backend API 1.19 and Rust 1.99. The API checks compatibility at backend startup. The examples below describe the 0.4.0 API. See CHANGELOG for release boundaries.

Crate 描述
triton-ng Safe backend API
triton-ng-client Async gRPC client
triton-ng-sys Raw FFI bindings
triton-ng-macros Backend and batching entry points

入门

[lib]
crate-type = ["cdylib"]

[dependencies]
triton-ng = "0.4.0"

Implement one hook to call another model and return its output. This complete backend is also examples/minimal-backend, the minimal backend example (the separate batching-strategy example is introduced below):

use triton_ng::{Context, CustomBackend, DataType, Error, InferenceRequest, Request, Response};

struct MyBackend;

#[triton_ng::backend]
impl CustomBackend for MyBackend {
    async fn model_instance_execute(ctx: Context, requests: Vec<Request>) -> Result<(), Error> {
        for request in requests {
            let data = request.get_input("INPUT")?.as_bytes()?;

            let mut inference = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
            inference.add_input_with_data("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], data)?;
            inference.add_requested_output("OUTPUT0")?;
            let result = match ctx.server().infer_async(inference).await {
                Ok(result) => result,
                Err(e) => {
                    request.respond_error_with_code(e.code(), &e.to_string())?;
                    continue;
                }
            };

            let mut response = Response::new(request)?;
            response
                .create_output("OUTPUT", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10])?
                .write_fp32_vec(&result.output("OUTPUT0")?.as_fp32_vec()?)?;
            response.send()?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}

gRPC client

Call the custom backend from your application using the gRPC client:

use triton_ng_client::{InferInput, InferOptions, TritonClient, TritonClientConfig};

type ClientError = Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>;

async fn call_example() -> Result<(), ClientError> {
    let client = TritonClient::new(TritonClientConfig::new("http://localhost:8001")).await?;
    let result = client.infer(
        "minimal_backend", None,
        [InferInput::fp32("INPUT", vec![1, 10], vec![1.0; 10])],
        ["OUTPUT"], InferOptions::default(),
    ).await?;
    for output in result.outputs {
        println!("{}: {:?}", output.name, output.data);
    }
    Ok(())
}

The examples below are independent functions or hooks; import their SDK types from triton_ng. Combine state fields when using several examples in one backend. make build compile-checks the Rust snippets in this README and every guide.

Compose models with BLS

Forward an input to another model without copying it:

async fn forward_input(ctx: &Context, request: &Request) -> Result<InferenceResult, Error> {
    let shared = request.get_input("INPUT")?.share()?;
    let mut call = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
    call.add_input_with_buffer("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], shared)?;
    call.add_requested_output("OUTPUT0")?;
    Ok(ctx.server().infer_async(call).await?)
}

To replace an input prepared by another helper and request only the embedding:

fn replace_audio(call: &mut InferenceRequest, samples: i64, audio: Vec<u8>) -> Result<(), Error> {
    call.remove_input("AUDIO")?;
    call.add_input_with_data("AUDIO", DataType::Fp32, &[1, samples], audio)?;
    call.remove_all_requested_outputs()?;
    call.add_requested_output("EMBEDDING")?;
    Ok(())
}

Request editing and buffer lifetimes.

流媒体

Return tokens as they become available. Configure the model with model_transaction_policy { decoupled: true }:

fn send_tokens(request: Request) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut sender = request.into_sender()?;
    for token in [10, 20, 30] {
        let mut response = sender.response()?;
        response.create_output("TOKEN", DataType::Int32, &[1])?.write_i32_vec(&[token])?;
        response.send()?;
    }
    sender.finish()?;
    Ok(())
}

Call a streaming model from another backend with Server::infer_stream, or from an application with TritonClient::infer_stream. See streaming and cancellation for complete examples.

Metrics and response statistics

Count completed requests on Triton's Prometheus endpoint. Create the counter once in model initialization and call count_request from execute:

fn model_initialize(model: &Model) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let name = model.name()?;
    let counter = CounterFamily::new("minimal_requests_total", "Requests handled")?
        .counter(&[("model", name.as_str())])?;
    model.set_state(counter)?;
    Ok(())
}

fn count_request(ctx: &Context) -> Result<(), Error> {
    ctx.state::<Counter>()?.increment(1.0)?;
    Ok(())
}

Request and batch statistics are automatic. Enable per-response statistics when needed:

fn answer_with_statistics(request: Request) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut response = Response::new(request)?;
    response.create_output("OUTPUT", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10])?.write_fp32_vec(&[0.0; 10])?;
    response.enable_statistics();
    response.send()?;
    Ok(())
}

Metric types, error responses, and statistics.

Tracing and metadata

Add a trace activity and connect a BLS call to its client request:

async fn traced_call(ctx: &Context, request: &Request) -> Result<InferenceResult, Error> {
    request.trace()?.report_activity("decode")?;
    let mut call = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
    call.set_parent_trace(request)?;
    if let Some(id) = request.id()? { call.set_id(&id)?; }
    call.set_parameter("language", "en")?;
    call.add_input_with_data("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], request.get_input("INPUT")?.as_bytes()?)?;
    Ok(ctx.server().infer_async(call).await?)
}

Request IDs, sequence flags, priority, timeouts, and tracing.

Memory buffers

Choose memory for each output, then take the buffers back for reuse. This example takes a prepared request for a model with three FP32 outputs of shape [1, 10]:

async fn reuse_outputs(
    ctx: &Context,
    mut call: InferenceRequest,
    device_id: i32,
) -> Result<(RamBuffer, PinnedRamBuffer, GpuBuffer), Error> {
    call.add_requested_output_into("CPU_OUTPUT", ctx.memory().ram(40)?)?;
    call.add_requested_output_into("PINNED_OUTPUT", ctx.memory().pinned(40)?)?;
    call.add_requested_output_into("GPU_OUTPUT", ctx.memory().gpu(device_id, 40)?)?;
    let mut result = ctx.server().infer_async(call).await?;
    Ok((
        result.take_ram("CPU_OUTPUT")?,
        result.take_pinned("PINNED_OUTPUT")?,
        result.take_gpu("GPU_OUTPUT")?,
    ))
}

Use any one of these buffer types, or combine them as above. Pinned and GPU allocations require Triton's corresponding memory pools. A GpuBuffer can become the next BLS call's input without a host copy; CPU access to its data requires your own CUDA code.

Report memory held by your model so clients can inspect it in model statistics:

fn model_initialize(model: &Model) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let allocation = model.memory_manager()?.pinned(4096)?;
    model.set_state(allocation)?;
    model.report_memory_usage(&[BufferAttributes::new(MemoryType::CpuPinned, 4096)?])?;
    Ok(())
}

For per-instance allocations use ModelInstance::report_memory_usage. Memory ownership, GPU chaining, and caching.

Configure backend and instances

Keep a setting shared by every model of your backend:

fn initialize(backend: &Backend) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let language = backend.config()?.parameter_or("language", String::from("en"))?;
    backend.set_state(language)?;
    backend.set_execution_policy(ExecutionPolicy::Blocking)?;
    let (_, directory) = backend.artifacts()?;
    println!("Backend files: {}", directory.display());
    Ok(())
}

fn language(ctx: &Context) -> Result<&str, Error> {
    Ok(ctx.backend_state::<String>()?.as_str())
}

Inspect an instance and save its host policy for later input reads:

fn model_instance_initialize(instance: &ModelInstance) -> Result<(), Error> {
    println!("{} passive={} profiles={:?} secondary={:?}",
        instance.name()?, instance.is_passive()?, instance.profile_names()?, instance.secondary_devices()?);
    instance.set_state(instance.host_policy()?)?;
    Ok(())
}

Backend configuration, execution policies, and instance settings.

Host-policy input data

Read the input storage selected for this instance:

fn read_policy(ctx: &Context, request: &Request) -> Result<Vec<u8>, Error> {
    let policy = ctx.instance_state::<HostPolicy>()?;
    request.get_input("INPUT")?.as_bytes_for_host_policy(policy.name())
}

Supply different input bytes for a BLS target's host policy:

fn policy_call(ctx: &Context, default: Vec<u8>, local: &[u8]) -> Result<InferenceRequest, Error> {
    let mut call = InferenceRequest::new(ctx.server(), "minimal_backend_target", -1)?;
    call.add_input_with_data("INPUT0", DataType::Fp32, &[1, 10], default)?;
    call.append_input_data_with_host_policy("INPUT0", local, "cpu")?;
    Ok(call)
}

Each input above contains ten FP32 values (40 bytes). A policy without supplied data uses the ordinary input. Policy selection and zero-copy appends.

Sequence state and iterative requests

Count requests in a sequence. Declare a state tensor with an initial value of zero, read its StateConfig with Model::sequence_states, then update it on each request:

fn increment(mut request: Request, config: &StateConfig) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let previous = request.get_input(config.input_name())?.as_fp32_vec()?;
    let previous = previous.first().copied().ok_or("state has no counter")?;
    let mut state = State::new(&mut request, config, &[1])?;
    state.write_bytes(&(previous + 1.0).to_ne_bytes())?;
    state.update()?;
    let mut response = Response::new(request)?;
    response.create_output("OUTPUT", DataType::Fp32, &[1])?.write_fp32_vec(&[previous + 1.0])?;
    response.send()?;
    Ok(())
}

This example uses max_batch_size: 0 and state dimensions [1]. Complete sequence-state configuration.

Return a partial result and schedule another step of a decoupled iterative sequence:

fn next_step(request: Request) -> Result<(), Error> {
    let mut sender = request.into_sender()?;
    let mut response = sender.response()?;
    response.create_output("STEP", DataType::Int32, &[1])?.write_i32_vec(&[1])?;
    response.send()?;
    sender.reschedule()?;
    Ok(())
}

Triton r25.09 allows only one reschedule per request; finish the response on the second step. Two-step execution and model configuration.

Custom batching

Group adjacent requests with the same batch_key parameter:

struct ByKey;
struct Batch { started: bool, key: Option<String> }

#[triton_ng::batch_strategy]
impl BatchStrategy for ByKey {
    type Batch = Batch;
    fn initialize(_model: &Model) -> Result<Self, Error> { Ok(Self) }
    fn batch(&self) -> Batch { Batch { started: false, key: None } }
    fn include(&self, batch: &mut Batch, request: &RequestView<'_>) -> Result<bool, Error> {
        let key = match request.parameter("batch_key")? {
            Some(Parameter::String(value)) => Some(value),
            _ => None,
        };
        if !batch.started {
            batch.started = true;
            batch.key = key;
            return Ok(true);
        }
        Ok(batch.key == key)
    }
}

Build this as a separate library and set TRITON_BATCH_STRATEGY_PATH in the model config. Runnable example · Queue behavior and safe model unload.

基准测试

The recorded benchmark compares five small BLS workloads on the same Triton 25.09 server, two CPU instances per backend, with a Ryzen 9 9950X3D. At concurrency 64:

工作量 triton-ng requests/s python_backend requests/s Ratio
Argmax, no BLS 119,907 52,716 2.27×
One BLS call 43,422 17,819 2.44×
Concurrent BLS calls 74,316 13,317 5.58×
Decoupled responses 12,802 3,670 3.49×
Consuming a BLS stream 15,056 3,253 4.63×

These are the recorded measurements, not a promise for large GPU models; heavy inference reduces the backend's share of total time. Streaming latency in these results is time to first response. Method, environment, all concurrency levels, and latency tables are in the benchmark guide.

发展

Install Rust, Docker, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and a compatible NVIDIA driver. The test suite also requires cargo-nextest. 从存储库根目录：

make build
make download-model
make docker-env-up
make tests
make docker-env-down

Wait until Triton reports the models ready before running the tests. After changing a backend, rebuild and restart the service. See the Makefile for all development commands.
